How do you program agency?

It’s a question I’ve been slightly obsessed with for the past few months. I’ve built automations that wake up every morning and ask me what’s on my mind. I’ve wired agents to monitor the news and text me when something interesting happens. I’ve been building an eval agent that gathers feedback on its own work and builds a backlog of what to do next.

I’m not alone. Boris Cherny, who runs Claude Code at Anthropic, half-jokes that his main job now is to write the loops that prompt Claude. 

Addy Osmani named the discipline: loop engineering. Design a system that discovers work, executes it, verifies the results, updates its own instructions, and repeats. Give an agent goals, skills, and permission to spin up subagents. Then let it loose while you go do something else (like doom scroll).

At least that’s the pitch. In practice, my loops meander constantly. Token costs balloon. Agents get stuck. One bad decision dominos until the system is grinding away, very confidently, in the wrong direction. And every time, I wondered if it was because the model isn’t smart enough. Maybe wait for the next release.

I think our recent obsession with loop engineering made me lean more towards

better models != better outcomes 

better systems = better outcomes

A loop is really a collection of jobs: 

• Orchestration
• Memory
• Verification
• Retrieval
• Routing

In practice, it could look something like this:

• Automations discover new work.

• Worktrees allow multiple agents to operate in parallel.

• Skills capture project-specific knowledge.

• Connectors give agents access to real systems.

• Sub-agents verify each other’s work.

• Persistent memory keeps state between runs.

Frontier intelligence matters most in two places: 

1/ orchestration, knowing when to break a problem apart or when to stop, and 

2/ self-modification, where the system rewrites its own instructions 

Roughly fewer than 10 percent of the tasks in my loops genuinely need frontier reasoning. The rest need better systems: memory design, retrieval structure, verification gates, context architecture. 

How does this change the economics of the frontier, which seem increasingly resource-intensive to create? 

Frontier intelligence is valuable and scarce. But increasingly it seems like moat it really has is a short window of time. 

Distillation dupes frontier capability within months at a fraction of the cost. 

The labs know this. This week, when Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5, it did so with anti-distillation defenses engineered into the model itself. Suspected distillation attempts get rerouted to an older model. Requests related to frontier model development were quietly degraded by invisible safeguards, a choice the company walked back after backlash. 

They care because their edge is temporal. While open models will likely never be first (they don’t have the copious amount of proprietary user data), they can always catch up to the latest, sometimes in weeks. 

This is maybe what makes the frontier race a finite game. 

Each generation is a round: ship the model, monetize the premium window, watch the capability get replicated, ship again. The labs can never stop playing. And the rounds get harder to win profitably. 

The volume underneath, meanwhile, explodes. And everyone starts feeling the burn of cost. Citadel’s Economics of Intelligence report goes into how AI adoption is becoming less about what models can do and more about the price of running them at scale. 

A lot of VC doomisms seems to be about how the frontier models are just going to build it all and that there’s nothing left to build. I think it’s the opposite: the frontier intelligence race will stay scarce and valuable. But it is playing a finite game: the labs have to win every round to stay in it.

I think the better position to be in would be those building the inference engineering infrastructure that runs underneath it all.

How to actually use Claude Fable, without burning your tokens.🔥

If you are blindly running Claude Fable 5 or specialized loop frameworks for your daily engineering tasks, you are setting yourself up for an astronomical API bill. 📉💰

Fable 5 is an absolute 10-trillion-parameter beast. But at $10 per million input tokens and a staggering $50 per million output tokens, letting it handle standard, low-leverage execution tasks is pure capital liquidation. 

To maximize frontier intelligence without hitting hard platform usage limits or draining your company's compute budget, you need a strict architectural strategy. 

Enter the **10/80/10 Hybrid System**. 

Here is how elite engineers are routing their workflows to extract 100% of Fable’s power at a fraction of the cost:

🏗️ The 10%: The Architect Phase (Fable 5)
Never use Fable 5 to write routine code or generic text blocks from scratch. Instead, use it exclusively at the very beginning of a project as your **Master Systems Architect**. 
• What to do: Feed Fable 5 your macro project goals, repository structures, and technical requirements. 
• The Output: Force the model to output a hyper-detailed, step-by-step structural blueprint, precise system specifications (`spec.md`), and modular prompt instructions for a lower-tier worker. You are paying the $50/M output fee only for high-leverage strategic planning.

⚙️ The 80%: The Worker Phase (Sonnet / Haiku / Local Models)
Once the master blueprint is compiled, swap out Fable entirely. You pass the `spec.md` and the modular sub-task scripts to highly efficient, cost-effective mid-tier models like Claude Sonnet or Haiku.
• What to do: Let the fast, cheap models handle the heavy lifting—writing the actual lines of code, parsing standard data blocks, formatting files, and compiling scripts based on Fable's rigid blueprint constraints. They do 80% of the mechanical, routine labor for a tiny fraction of the API cost.

🔍 The 10%: The Critic Phase (Fable 5)
Once the worker models have generated the code or assets, you bring Fable 5 back into the loop for the final mile. It acts as your **Master Quality Critic & Security Red-Teamer**.
• What to do: Feed the generated assets back to Fable 5. Have it scan the code for subtle logic gaps, hidden security vulnerabilities, or architectural deviations from the original `spec.md`. It reviews, approves, and polishes the final 10% before deployment.

🛠️ Official Guardrails for `/loop` and `/goal` Commands
When utilizing advanced terminal utilities like Claude Code, the native background loops can run completely wild, spinning up dozens of multi-agent turns that burn through your token tier limits in minutes. Implement these operational safety guardrails:
1️⃣ Set Hard Effort Dials: Always initialize Fable on the *lowest possible thinking effort setting*. Only dial up the cognitive compute when a lower-tier worker completely fails an execution check.
2️⃣ Bound the Budget: Never execute an open-ended loop command (like `sloop keep building until complete`) without a hard operational circuit breaker. Force the system to halt after a maximum of 3 to 5 multi-agent turns for human inspection.

The Takeaway:
Model routing and multi-tier engineering are no longer optional. The game isn't about using the "best" model for everything—it’s about knowing how to orchestrate a hierarchy of models. By using Fable 5 strictly as the Architect and the Critic, while forcing mid-tier engines to act as the raw labor, you get production-grade frontier outputs without the enterprise-level token hangover. 🖥️🛡️

Has anyone compared Fable 5’s game development capabilities with GPT-5.5?

I’ve been seeing a lot of posts about Fable 5’s ability to build games, but I’m curious about comparisons with GPT-5.5. 

Not in terms of simple 1-shot performance, but based on much deeper, more interactive workflows over a longer session.

A user on Reddit shared a MineBench comparison between Claude Fable 5 and Opus 4.8, and the results are honestly pretty interesting.

Fable 5 averaged ~18 mins inference time, while Opus 4.8 took almost ~25 mins on average.

Which is funny because on Claude, Fable actually feels slower and like it thinks forever 

The cost numbers were interesting too:
Fable 5 → $54.93 for 15 builds
Opus 4.8 → $41.52 for 15 builds

And this is despite Fable’s API pricing being 2x more expensive than Opus 4.8.

So the benchmark creator thinks Fable is probably generating way fewer tokens overall, which is helping keep the cost relatively lower.

What’s also interesting is that the builds apparently weren’t some gigantic leap over GPT 5.5 Pro visually, but Fable showed insane attention to tiny details.

One example was a Pac-Man arcade build where it correctly added the game screen, score counter, and even the “1UP” label

Also apparently adding prompts like:
“LEVEL OF DETAIL: MAXIMUM”
“BOUNDING BOX: UNLIMITED”

improved the outputs a lot.

Benchmarks are slowly becoming half model eval and half prompting skill issue at this point.

I have a keen interest in Spacetech. In fact, I have even invested in a solid Spacetech startup here in India (Will share more on that another day). The global focus today is on SpaceX’s IPO.

The reported numbers are very interesting
-Expected IPO price: $135/share
-Raise: ~$75B at  ~$1.75T valuation
-Demand: 3.5 to 4x oversubscribed
-Retail access: Up to 30% retail allocation

While the scale is massive, what genuinely excites me isn't just the size of the IPO. It is how and where the price discovery is happening. 

For decades, IPO pricing was a closed-door game controlled by bankers and a few privileged institutions.
But thanks to crypto rails, @SpaceX-linked perpetual futures have been trading publicly, 24/7, since mid-May.

Look at the public data:
– SPCX futures trading around $173.5 this morning vs. the $135 IPO price 
– A ~29% premium discovered before the bell even rings – Over $3.2B in cumulative volume and ~$390M in open interest.  

An important note: These are synthetic perps, not actual SpaceX shares (meaning no ownership or voting rights). But they prove an important point. Crypto markets are creating a live, liquid, and democratic signal of what the market actually thinks an asset is worth.

And the track record is honest, not perfect: Airbnb's futures undershot the 2020 pop. Coinbase's overshot at peak mania in 2021. But just last month, these markets called the Cerebras opening price within ~1.3%. As liquidity deepens, the signal sharpens. (Image generated via Claude Fable 5. In the comments)

Yes, three data points is a small sample. But the direction is unmistakable. We are shifting to an era where price discovery happens continuously, in public, weeks in advance! Later today, we find out how accurate the crowd's math is this time on SpaceX. 

But one thing is crystal clear: Price discovery is finally becoming public infrastructure and it will only get better when more people start participating in these global markets.
